Here’s a post about what actually affects whether people want to follow you in the first place.

1. Mutual followers

There’s a good – and, importantly, independent – study from last year that looked at the factors influencing the likelihood of someone following a person on LinkedIn.

The conclusion: users were much more likely to follow people they shared a large number of second-degree connections with.

In other words, people are more likely to follow when they see that their professional circle has already validated this person.

A similar dynamic exists on X.

And this is exactly why I emphasized that relationships and networking are critical for growth in my Telegram channel for founders and marketers

(worth your follow btw https://t.co/EOvweTclpo)

Because if a user sees “not followed by anyone you follow,” there’s a pretty good chance they’ll simply move on.

2. Content.

Broadly speaking, there are two types:

• Expert content – which is exactly what you’re reading right now, or at least what I’m trying to make it

• Emotional content – a meme about meat proxies, or some random thoughts about the meaning of life

Emotional content usually gets more likes.

But statistically, it does not drive meaningful growth in a relevant, long-term audience – while expert content tends to have the longest conversion tail when it comes to new followers.

thread_tweets.text:
3. Focus.

When you try to write about everything at once – especially at the early stages of growth – the value of following you goes down.

The potential reader simply doesn’t know what to expect from you.

And if they don’t know what to expect, they have no real reason to add you to their feed.

So it usually makes sense to start with a narrow area of expertise where you genuinely have something to say — and then occasionally expand into adjacent topics through market commentary.

At the end of the day, following someone is an investment of attention.

People invest that attention into content that helps them make money, grow professionally, or better understand what’s happening around them.

The dopamine rollercoaster can stay on Instagram and TikTok ;)

#Uranium #Silver #Copper #Gold

DAILY METALS PULSE | 21 September 2026

A new week brings fresh catalysts: China’s yuan is strengthening, nuclear construction is advancing, and precious-metals sentiment is improving. Interest rates remain the challenge.

☢️ URANIUM
China’s Lufeng 5 has completed containment integrity tests, according to Friday’s update, with operations expected in 2027. Its sister unit is expected to follow in 2028.

Each construction milestone brings another source of long-term fuel demand closer. For me, that steady expansion of the reactor fleet remains central to the uranium investment case.

🥈 SILVER
CPM Group flagged fresh short-term buy signals for silver and gold on Friday. This week’s flash manufacturing PMIs offer another test for silver’s industrial outlook.

I’m watching new orders alongside input costs. Stronger demand with easing inflation pressure would be a supportive combination; hotter inflation could keep interest-rate expectations working against the metal.

🔶 COPPER
The yuan reached its strongest level against the dollar in more than three and a half years this morning, ahead of Thursday’s Trump–Xi summit.

My read: a stronger yuan improves Chinese purchasing power for dollar-priced copper, all else equal. Progress on trade could provide another boost, although a major agreement is far from assured.

🥇 GOLD
All 16 analysts in Kitco’s latest weekly survey expect gold to rise this week. That’s a striking improvement in sentiment, though a small survey cannot establish the market’s direction.

I remain bullish on gold’s role in protecting purchasing power through policy uncertainty. The immediate test is whether buying interest can withstand renewed pressure from rates and the dollar.

📅 WATCH THIS WEEK
Wednesday: flash PMIs.
Thursday: Trump–Xi summit and US jobless claims.
Friday: US durable goods and consumer sentiment.

My longer-term conviction in all four remains strong. This week, I’m watching whether the economic data and policy headlines support it.

The reason so many people look for an ulterior motive for the AI labs asking to be regulated is that they don't grasp that models could be dangerous. But if you try assuming models are getting dangerous, or at least unpredictable, everything falls into place.

If models are getting dangerous, you want to slow down. But you don't want to slow down unilaterally and be left behind. So you ask the government to make your competitors slow down too. And you can't do that with a straight face without asking to be regulated yourself.

tweets.text:
𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗧𝗪𝗢 𝗟𝗘𝗩𝗘𝗟𝗦 𝗢𝗙 𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗟𝗜𝗧𝗬

There are two levels of reality.

The first level is reality as it exists.

There are wars, politics, sickness, disease, murder and death. People behave in ways we do not like. A tiger kills another animal for food. A dog eats a baby rabbit.

At this first level, these things simply happen. Before the mind calls them good or bad, they are facts of reality. 

This does not mean that we should support war, ignore suffering or stop trying to prevent injustice. It simply means that reality has already happened before our mind judges it.

Then there is the second level: what the mind believes reality should be.

There should be no war.
This political party should win.
That person should behave differently.
I should not be sick.
I should have more money.
My relationship should have worked.
The cupboard should be closed.

Human beings have a will. We want reality to be a certain way.

When reality agrees with our will, we feel happy. We want a girlfriend and find one. We want money and make it. We want success and achieve it.

But this happiness usually lasts only for a while. Soon the will finds something else that is missing.

When reality does not agree with our will, we become unhappy. Sometimes we remain unhappy for months or even years.

But who decided what must happen for us to be happy?

One day, I noticed that the cupboard under my television was open. Immediately, a thought appeared:

It should be closed.

I did not consciously create this thought. It simply arose. Along with it came a small feeling of discomfort and the desire to close the cupboard.

If I closed it, I would feel better. But only because my will had decided that a closed cupboard was right and an open cupboard was wrong.

So instead, I left it open.

At first, it was frustrating. My will continued telling me to close it. But I could observe the desire without obeying it.

Slowly, the discomfort became weaker. Eventually, I could look at the open cupboard and understand that nothing was wrong. It was simply open.

The important lesson was not about the cupboard. It was about my relationship with my own will.

I can control whether I close a cupboard. But I cannot always control sickness, war, politics, money, success, relationships or death.

The cupboard is therefore a place to practise.

I leave it open and allow the discomfort to exist. I see that the desire to close it arises by itself. I do not fight the desire, but I also do not have to obey it.

Each time I do this, the will becomes a little less powerful. I begin to understand that reality does not need to follow my preferences for me to be at peace.

This does not mean becoming passive. I can still close the cupboard when it is useful. I can try to cure disease, prevent war, build a relationship and improve my life.

The difference is that I act without demanding that reality obey me.

Suffering begins in the space between what exists and what the mind insists should exist. Freedom begins when we can see both levels clearly.

Reality is what happens.

The second level is the story we tell ourselves about how it should have happened.

We may not be able to control the first level. But we can slowly stop being ruled by the second.

Start with your cupboard.

one more bull market tip since people have been enjoying this series - OG followers of mine have probably heard this a million times. Good ol' GCR & Howard Marks: 

1. "Try to think your ponzis as prizefighters rather than coins; winners win and losers lose"

I would not advocate selling your winners to add to bags that "haven't pumped". Howard Marks talks about this (and it's one of my favourite quotes): 

- Why sell something you think has a positive long-term future to prepare for a dip you expect to be temporary?
- Doing so introduces one more way to be wrong (of which there are so many), since the decline might not occur.
- Charlie Munger, vice chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, points out that selling for market-timing purposes actually gives an investor two ways to be wrong: the decline may or may not occur, and if it does, you’ll have to figure out when the time is right to go back in.
- Or maybe it’s three ways, because once you sell, you also have to decide what to do with the proceeds while you wait until the dip occurs and the time comes to get back in.
- People who avoid declines by selling too often may revel in their brilliance and fail to reinstate their positions at the resulting lows.  Thus, even sellers who were right can fail to accomplish anything of lasting value.
- Lastly, what if you’re wrong and there is no dip?  In that case, you’ll miss out on the ensuing gains and either never get back in or do so at higher prices.

Jev is a textbook example of Clayton Christensen’s Innovator’s Dilemma playing out in AI.

It is commoditizing the bottom of the ML market: classifiers, routers, scoring and context triage. For frontier LLM labs, these workloads are not even worth pursuing. Revenue per decision is tiny, margins are razor-thin, and their entire infrastructure is optimized around selling expensive reasoning and token generation.

They cannot simply put a smaller LLM on fast inference chips like Cerebras and compete. Jev uses fundamentally different infrastructure, built to return typed probabilistic decisions so it’s a pure disruption
